How would they inhale and exhale when underwater?
It's pretty easy to exhale while under water, but yeah, inhaling might be a bit tricky.
Im pretty sure humans don't get the bends when they free dive either... Its only when attached to a scuba tank that this occurs.

Doing very deep and repeated free dives can cause the bends. The nitrogen build up during dives does not have time to vent out during a rapid ascend and can cause decompression sickness (DCS), especially if you do not give the nitrogen time to vent between dives. There are experimental dive tables for free diving beeing developed. I do not free dive anymore so I'm a bit out of touch. I found on article on the subject here.

The bends is caused by having too much nitrogen dissolved in your blood when breathing air at deep pressures, which would form bubbles upon ascending. I don't see how that would ever affect dolphins, or what it has to do with lung capacity.

I can't be arsed to look for sources, but some marine animals actually exhale before a dive. This minimizes the extra nitrogen being dissolved in the bloodstream during deep dives. I can't remember the name, but there is a seal doing this and I think the sperm whale.

Those animals have a large spleen that contains oxygenated blood that are released into the bloodstream during deep dives. It is called the "dive response" which also slows the heart and switches large parts of the body to aenarobic mode producing lactic acid instead. Humans also have the dive response, to a much lesser degree of course. If you have access to a pulse meter, try the following: (not alone, silly) Put it on and note your pulse. Do this standing up. Now take a deep breath and start walking, slowly. After a while it will start to be very hard to hold your breath anymore. No worries, you can hold it for at least as long again. It is hard going though. After a while you should start seeing a drop in pulse and a tired feeling in your extremities. This is the dive response kicking in. The dive response is stronger if your face is cold and wet and deep under water (high pressure). Pretty cool, eh?
